messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 79
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Warehouse Worker
- Trauma Type: Combat
- Pcl5: 65

He is a 79-year-old South Asian man who comes to the work of therapy carrying a life that has already outlived many of the people and places that shaped him. When he speaks about the war, he does so in a measured voice, as if he is still trying to keep the worst parts of it contained. He was a young man when he entered combat, strong enough then to believe he could endure anything if he stayed useful and kept moving. What he remembers most is not a single battle but the long accumulation of fear: the smell of diesel and dust, the metallic taste in his mouth before shelling, the silence that followed explosions, and the constant effort of watching for danger even while his body begged for rest.

He describes how, in those years, sleep was never complete. He learned to wake instantly at the smallest sound, and that vigilance became part of him. There were moments when he saw men fall before he could understand what had happened, and afterward he carried the image of their bodies with him like a burden he never set down. He does not speak of these events melodramatically. Instead, he tells them with the flatness of someone who had to survive by pushing emotion aside. Even now, decades later, he can still feel his heart kick hard in his chest when a door slams unexpectedly or when a vehicle backfires nearby. His body reacts before his mind can catch up, and the old alertness returns with a force that surprises him.

After the war, he tries to build an ordinary life. He marries, has work to do, children to raise, and for many years he tells himself that what happened overseas belongs to the past. He takes jobs that ask little of speech and much of endurance, eventually settling into warehouse work, where he appreciates the routine, the physical labor, and the fact that the lifting and sorting keep his hands busy. He likes knowing where things belong and moving them into order. The predictable rhythm helps him feel less exposed. Still, even in the warehouse, certain sounds throw him off balance. A forklift revving sharply or metal shelving crashing can make him freeze for a second too long. He covers by pretending to check an inventory sheet or bend to pick up a box, but inside he is already bracing for impact.

His marriage ends years ago, and he speaks of the divorce with little bitterness, though there is a tiredness in him when the subject comes up. He says he was often distant, quick to retreat into himself, and hard for others to know. He does not deny it. He remembers becoming irritable over small things, especially when he felt cornered or when someone stood too close behind him. He would rather withdraw than explain. Over time, his family learned that he was the kind of man who missed gatherings, sat with his back to the wall, and rarely talked about the past. He keeps his emotions contained so tightly that even grief seems to arrive sideways, in his jaw, his shoulders, or the stiffness in his hands.

In recent years, the old memories have become harder to manage. He finds himself replaying scenes from combat at night, especially when the house is quiet and he is alone with his thoughts. Sleep comes lightly and breaks easily. He drifts off and then wakes with a start, disoriented, listening for sounds that are not there. Some mornings he feels as if he has spent the night fighting rather than resting. When an image returns, it is not always vivid in a visual sense; sometimes it is the feeling of fear itself, immediate and physical, as if danger is just beyond the room. He avoids news about war and turns away from anything that reminds him too much of the past. At the same time, he says he cannot fully stop remembering. Certain smells, certain voices, the sight of uniforms or injured bodies on television pull him back without warning.

There are days when he moves through the warehouse with practiced competence, but his attention is divided. He checks and rechecks tasks, not because he is careless, but because part of him is always scanning. He tires more easily now. At 79, his body no longer recovers as quickly, and he feels the weight of years in his knees and back. Still, the greater exhaustion comes from carrying a mind that never fully stands down. He speaks of wanting peace, though he is not always sure he knows how to feel it. What he knows is that the war did not end when he came home. It settled into his sleep, his reflexes, his relationships, and the private spaces of his daily life, where it continues to appear in the smallest moments and quietly shape the way he moves through the world.
